question: How do we define LLM evals, and what are the key characteristics?
reference_answer: LLM evals are systematic, repeatable tests used to judge an LLM or LLM-powered system against clear criteria. Systematic means proper datasets covering edge cases instead of a few ad hoc questions. Repeatable means the same test can be re-run after changing the prompt, model, retriever or chunking to compare versions. Criteria means you define in advance what good looks like.
claims: LLM evals are systematic repeatable tests that judge an LLM or LLM-powered system against clear criteria
Systematic means using proper datasets that cover edge cases, not vibe testing
Repeatable means the same eval can be re-run after changing prompt, model, retriever or chunking strategy
Repeatability lets you compare version 1 against version 2 on the same dataset
Clear criteria (e.g. correct, simple, grounded in course content, safe) are defined up front

question: What are application evals and why do they matter if we already have model evals?
reference_answer: Application evals assess the behaviour and performance of an LLM-powered application, either as a whole system or at the level of one component. The LLM is only one component next to the UI, prompts, tools, orchestration code, guardrails, parsers, memory, retrieval and monitoring, so a strong model alone does not guarantee a good product. Model evals ask whether a model can do something; application evals ask whether the product works.
claims: Application evals assess an LLM-powered application at whole-system level or component level
The LLM is just one component among prompts, tools, orchestration, guardrails, memory, retrieval and monitoring
A good model does not guarantee a good application (like a strong processor does not guarantee a good smartphone)
Model evals ask whether the model can do a task, application evals ask whether the product works
Frontier labs evaluate models but AI engineers are responsible for evaluating the systems they build

question: What is a golden dataset and how is one created?
reference_answer: A golden dataset is the evaluation dataset of inputs paired with manually labelled correct outputs. It usually has 50 to 500 rows and is best built from real past data, labelled by people, and it should cover edge cases. Failures found in production are later added to it.
claims: A golden dataset pairs inputs with manually labelled expected outputs
It is usually around 50 to 500 rows
It is best built from real past data labelled manually by people
It should cover many cases including edge cases
Production failures get added to it over time

question: What are the three levels at which an LLM application can fail and be evaluated?
reference_answer: Component level (e.g. retriever, reranker, embedding model, system prompt, parser, tool selector, memory, guardrails), workflow level (how components interact, e.g. the retriever-generator combination in RAG) and application level (whole-system properties such as latency, token cost and time to first token).
claims: Component level covers individual parts like retriever, reranker, embedding model, system prompt, output parser, agent tool selector, memory and guardrails
Workflow level covers the interaction between components, such as the retriever and generator in RAG
Application level covers whole-system properties such as latency, token cost and time to first token

question: What are the risk categories in LLM evaluation?
reference_answer: Risks are grouped into application quality (does the app do its job: correct, relevant, complete, instruction-following answers), safety (no toxic, harmful, biased content, no PII leaks, resistance to prompt injection and jailbreaks) and operations (latency, cost per request, token efficiency, error rate, latency under load). Specific risks differ for RAG, agents and multi-turn chatbots.
claims: The three risk categories are quality, safety and operations
Quality covers correctness, relevance, completeness and instruction following
Safety covers toxicity, harmful content, bias, PII leakage and prompt injection/jailbreak resistance
Operations covers latency, cost per request, token efficiency, error rate and latency under load

RAG adds context relevance, retrieval recall, groundedness and citation accuracy; agents add tool selection, parameter correctness, task completion and error recovery; multi-turn chatbots add context retention and clarification behaviour

question: What are the different eval methods and who actually executes the evaluation?
reference_answer: An eval method is the mechanism that decides whether an output is good. There are three: programmatic/deterministic (code computes the result), human (people grade) and model-graded (an LLM does it, commonly called LLM-as-a-judge). Whatever the pipeline, one of these three executes it.
claims: An eval method is the mechanism that turns an output into a judgement
The three methods are programmatic (deterministic), human and model/LLM-graded
The method answers who runs the evaluation: a program, a human or an LLM
LLM-as-a-judge is the popular technique for model-graded evaluation

question: When should I use LLM-as-a-judge instead of code or humans?
reference_answer: Use it when the quality is too nuanced to compute with a program but humans would be too costly at scale. Humans are reliable but expensive; programs are cheap but can't judge things like helpfulness or long answers; an LLM judge sits in between. It is given a rubric and its results can be compared against human-labelled scores to check agreement.
claims: Programmatic checks cannot handle nuanced or long-text judgements like comparing paragraphs semantically
Humans are more reliable but costly, especially at scale
LLM-as-a-judge is the middle option combining some qualities of both
The judge is given a rubric and instructions
Its output can be validated against human scores (e.g. via mean absolute error) with the goal of minimising deviation

question: What are offline evals and what are their main benefits?
reference_answer: Offline evals are eval pipelines run on the application before deployment. Their three main benefits are pre-release testing (which can act as a release gate), version comparison (run the same eval on different prompts, models, re-rankers or architectures), and regression testing (checking that improving one thing did not break another).
claims: Offline eval means running an eval pipeline on the application before deploying it
Benefit 1: pre-release testing before launch
Benefit 2: comparing versions (models, prompts, re-rankers, vector databases, architectures) on the same eval
Benefit 3: regression testing so changes don't degrade other behaviour

question: What is drift and why does it make my offline eval setup obsolete?
reference_answer: Drift means the real world changes while the eval setup stays the same. As business documents, prices or policies change, or user expectations change, the golden dataset (built for the old distribution) no longer represents reality, so offline scores stay good while users become unhappy. Types include data drift, concept drift (expectation/purpose mismatch), model drift and user drift; it can't be controlled, only detected.
claims: Drift is change in data, users or expectations over time while the eval setup stays fixed
The golden dataset reflects the distribution at creation time and becomes outdated
Offline evals can keep passing while real users give negative feedback
Drift has multiple types including data drift, concept drift and model drift
Drift cannot be controlled in AI systems and must be monitored

question: What is online eval and why does it not need a golden dataset?
reference_answer: Online eval evaluates the system on live production traffic after deployment, as real users interact with it. Since you can't know in advance what users will ask or the correct answer, it works without a golden dataset or answer key, using reference-free evaluators, user signals and baseline comparisons.
claims: Online eval runs on live production traffic after deployment
It works without an answer key or golden dataset
It has to estimate quality on the fly since the inputs cannot be anticipated
It catches drift, emergent bugs and surprises that offline eval can't

question: How do I evaluate quality in production when I don't have the correct answers?
reference_answer: Use metrics that don't need ground truth, such as faithfulness, where an LLM judge sees the retrieved context and the answer and checks whether the answer is grounded. Use user signals such as thumbs-down spikes as proxies for correctness, and compare current metric distributions against a baseline to detect abnormal behaviour.
claims: Some metrics such as faithfulness need only the context and answer, not a correct answer
An LLM can judge such reference-free metrics
Thumbs up/down and similar user feedback proxy for correctness
Comparing with a baseline (from earlier weeks or offline evals) reveals abnormal changes

question: What is a benchmark and what does it consist of?
reference_answer: A benchmark is a standardized, shared test that measures a specific model capability. It has four parts: a dataset/task (questions with answer keys), a run configuration (how the test must be run), a scoring method, and an aggregation method. Benchmarks are usually published in research papers.
claims: A benchmark is a standardized test of a specific model capability
Component 1: dataset and task with questions and answers
Component 2: run configuration
Component 3: scoring method
Component 4: aggregation method
Benchmarks generally originate from research papers that specify these details

question: What is an eval harness and why use one?
reference_answer: An eval harness is the plumbing code that runs a model through a benchmark loop: building prompts, calling the model, extracting answers, scoring, batching, retries and rate limits. Libraries such as lm-evaluation-harness, Inspect and HELM provide it, so you don't write and standardise it yourself. Analogy: the benchmark is the exam paper, the harness is the exam administration.
claims: The benchmark loop is: load item, build prompt, call model with fixed settings, extract answer, score, store, then aggregate
Running it reliably at thousands of calls needs extra engineering: extraction, batching, retries and rate limits
That plumbing code is called an eval harness
Libraries like lm-evaluation-harness, Inspect and HELM provide it
Benchmark = exam paper, harness = exam administration

question: What is benchmark contamination?
reference_answer: Contamination happens when a public benchmark's questions and answers end up in a model's training data, so the model may have memorised answers instead of demonstrating capability. It mainly affects public, static benchmarks; private and dynamic benchmarks are the mitigations.
claims: Public benchmark data can be scraped into the pre-training data of later models
The model may then answer from memorisation rather than real ability
Older public static benchmarks are especially affected
Solutions include private benchmarks and dynamic benchmarks whose data updates

question: What does MMLU measure, and what does it not measure?
reference_answer: MMLU (2020) measures breadth of knowledge with about 14,000 multiple-choice questions (4 options) across 57 subjects. It does not measure reasoning depth, calibration (whether a model knows what it doesn't know), open-ended answering or multilingual ability. Known issues: about 6.5% wrong labels (capping scores near 92-93%), contamination, and sensitivity to prompt format.
claims: MMLU tests breadth of knowledge with ~14,000 four-option MCQs over 57 subjects
It does not test reasoning depth, calibration, open-ended generation or multilinguality
About 6.5% of questions have errors, so no model can reach 100%
It is heavily contaminated
Results are sensitive to prompt format, so conditions must be identical when comparing models

question: What is GPQA and why is it called Google-proof?
reference_answer: GPQA is a science benchmark (physics, chemistry, biology) of PhD-level questions validated by two domain experts, so hard that a non-expert with Google access can't solve them in about 30 minutes. It has main (443), extended (546) and diamond (198) subsets, and headline scores usually refer to the hardest diamond set. Its small size lowers statistical confidence.
claims: It tests depth of knowledge in physics, chemistry and biology with expert-level questions
Each question is validated by two domain experts
A non-expert with Google can't solve them in 30 minutes, hence Google-proof
It has main, extended and diamond subsets, with diamond being the hardest (198 questions)
Few questions means low confidence in results

question: Why shouldn't I blindly trust LLM leaderboards?
reference_answer: Benchmark performance may not transfer to messy real applications; benchmarks may be contaminated; models can be over-optimised for the leaderboard (Goodhart's law: a measure that becomes a target stops being a good measure); composite leaderboards hide which benchmarks and weights are used; small score gaps and ranks are misleading; human-preference leaderboards carry human bias; and scores can be stale, incomplete or self-reported.
claims: Benchmark performance may not transfer to real applications with messy inputs
Contaminated benchmarks inflate leaderboard scores
Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure, and models get over-optimised for leaderboards
Benchmark selection and weighting in composite scores may be opaque
Small score differences don't justify rank differences
Human preference leaderboards have human biases such as liking long confident answers
Leaderboard scores can be stale, incomplete or self-reported

question: What's the process for choosing an LLM for my application using custom model evals?
reference_answer: Three stages: (1) gather requirements (task, cost ceiling, latency, context, deployment, correctness); (2) use leaderboards to shortlist 5-10 candidate models that meet those requirements; (3) run a custom model eval on your own golden dataset and task across the candidates, and pick the best based on the results.
claims: Stage 1: write down requirements for the application
Stage 2: shortlist 5 to 10 candidate models from leaderboards using those requirements
Stage 3: run a custom eval on your own data across all candidates
Leaderboards are used for filtering, not final selection
The best model on your own eval is chosen

question: What is the RAG triad?
reference_answer: The RAG triad is the three metrics between the question, retrieved context and answer: context relevance (is the retrieved context relevant to the question), faithfulness (is the answer grounded in the context rather than hallucinated) and answer relevance (does the answer address the question). If all three hold, the RAG pipeline is working properly.
claims: Context relevance relates question and context
Faithfulness relates answer and context
Answer relevance relates answer and question
Together they evaluate the RAG pipeline

question: What is regression testing for an LLM app and what levels of it exist?
reference_answer: Regression testing runs your eval suite to check that a new version is not worse than the previous one. Level 1 runs the suite and compares against a baseline manually; level 2 adds experiment tracking (e.g. MLflow) with a dashboard logging configurations and metrics per run; level 3 adds CI so a new change is automatically evaluated and blocked if metrics fall below the baseline or threshold.
claims: Regression testing means running the eval suite to check the new version isn't worse than the old
Level 1: run the suite and compare with baseline numbers manually
Level 2: experiment tracking with a dashboard (e.g. MLflow) of configs and metrics
Level 3: CI runs evals automatically and gates deployment on thresholds or baseline
On success the baseline is updated to the new metrics

question: How do offline evals, deployment, online evals and the golden dataset fit together as one loop?
reference_answer: You build and iterate on the system using offline evals against a golden dataset, deploy once it clears the bar, then monitor with online evals on live traffic. Failures found in production are added to the golden dataset (e.g. via add-to-dataset or annotation queues), so the next offline run is richer, and the cycle repeats for as long as the system is deployed.
claims: Offline evals on a golden dataset are used to iterate before deployment
After deployment, online evals monitor live production traffic
Failures seen in production are added back to the golden dataset
Annotation queues and add-to-dataset in tools like LangSmith help close the loop
The loop continues as long as the system is deployed, making the golden dataset richer

question: What does a golden dataset contain for different kinds of evals (classification, retrieval, LLM-judge grading, text-to-SQL)?
reference_answer: It depends on the task. For classification it holds inputs with labelled correct classes; for retriever evals it holds questions with the IDs of relevant documents identified by a human expert; for LLM-judge grading it holds answers with human-assigned marks according to a rubric; for text-to-SQL it holds questions with validated gold SQL queries. Datasets without an answer key are used for reference-free evals.
claims: Classification: inputs with manually labelled correct classes
Retriever eval: questions with relevant document IDs marked by a human expert
LLM-judge grading: answers with human marks against a rubric
Custom model eval for text-to-SQL: questions with validated golden queries
Reference-free evals need only inputs (like questions) and no answer key

question: Where does LLM-as-a-judge show up across the course and what are its limitations?
reference_answer: It is used to grade subjective outputs (such as UPSC-style answers against a rubric), as a reference-free evaluator for online metrics like hallucination, and to score open-ended benchmark answers (TruthfulQA generation, SimpleQA, HLE). Limitations: it is costly at scale, can make grading errors, and as judge models improve over time, scores from an older judge can't be directly compared with newer ones.
claims: LLM judges grade subjective work using a rubric and are validated against human scores
They act as reference-free evaluators in online evals (e.g. hallucination)
They are used to grade open-ended benchmark answers such as SimpleQA and HLE, and to extract answers in TruthfulQA
Running them on all production traffic is expensive, so sampling is used
Judge quality changes over time, making benchmark results from different eras not directly comparable
Judge grading errors can vary results

question: How do I evaluate a retriever, and what metrics do I use?
reference_answer: Use a golden dataset of questions with human-marked relevant documents, run the retriever with top-K, and compute recall@K (how many relevant documents were retrieved) and precision (how many retrieved documents were useful), matched by document ID and averaged over the dataset. If scores are poor, improve the embedding model, expand queries, increase K, or add a re-ranker.
claims: Recall measures how many of the right documents were retrieved
Precision measures how many of the retrieved documents were useful
Evaluation matches retrieved IDs against golden relevant IDs and averages across questions
A human expert creates the golden relevance labels
Improvements include a better embedding model, query expansion, larger K and re-ranking

question: What is faithfulness (groundedness) and how is it used across offline, online and RAG evaluation?
reference_answer: Faithfulness checks that an answer is generated from the provided context with no invented facts. It needs only context and answer, no golden answer, so it works as a reference-free metric: used for the generator component, as one third of the RAG triad, and online as a computed signal by an LLM judge on sampled production chats.
claims: Faithfulness/groundedness means the answer is based on the retrieved context with nothing extra added
It doesn't require a correct reference answer
It is used to evaluate the generator and forms one part of the RAG triad
Online, it is computed by an evaluator over sampled conversations
Its baseline from offline evals can be compared with live values

question: How does regression testing connect offline evals, baselines and CI?
reference_answer: Offline evals guard against regression: after a change, you re-run the same golden dataset (covering different question types) to check nothing got worse. In the RAG suite this becomes regression testing, comparing the new version's metrics with the baseline, tracking experiments and configs, and letting a CI tool gate deployment when scores drop below the threshold.
claims: Improving one thing can degrade another, so evals should be re-run across question types
Regression tests compare new-version metrics against a baseline
Experiment tracking logs configs and metrics for each run
CI can automatically gate deployment based on thresholds
The baseline is updated when the new version is better

question: How do multiple failure points and risk categories translate into an actual RAG eval suite?
reference_answer: Failure points map to levels: retriever and generator components get their own evals, their interaction gets the RAG triad at pipeline level, and the whole application gets its own evals. Risk categories map to quality (correctness, completeness, style), safety (toxicity, PII, jailbreak) and operations (latency, cost, tokens). Together they form the eval suite.
claims: Retriever and generator are evaluated separately at component level
The RAG triad evaluates their interaction at pipeline level
Application-level evals include correctness, completeness and style
Safety evals include toxicity, PII leakage and jailbreak resistance
Operations evals include latency, cost and tokens

question: What's the full workflow from benchmarks to choosing a model for my app?
reference_answer: Benchmarks and leaderboards give general capability information and help filter candidates, but they are not decision tools. Gather your application's requirements, use leaderboards to shortlist about 5-10 models within cost and latency limits, then run a custom eval on your own golden dataset and pick the best one, which may differ from the top-ranked model.
claims: Benchmarks test generic capabilities in standardised conditions
Leaderboards aggregate benchmark results and are a filtering tool, not a decision tool
Requirements (cost, latency, context, deployment, correctness) constrain the shortlist
5 to 10 candidates are shortlisted and tested on a custom golden dataset
The winning model is decided by the custom eval, not by rank alone

question: Why aren't benchmark scores and leaderboard rankings enough to pick a model?
reference_answer: Benchmarks measure generic capabilities on clean data and can be contaminated, saturated, gamed through favourable configurations, or hide weak subjects behind averages. They also ignore cost and latency for your task. A custom eval on your data can show a cheaper model performing almost as well, or a hyped model being slow and inaccurate, so custom evals are needed.
claims: A model that wins every benchmark may not be the best value for a specific task
Benchmarks can be contaminated, saturated, gamed and aggregated misleadingly
Real applications involve messy data, cost and latency constraints that benchmarks ignore
Custom evals on your own data show task-specific accuracy, cost and latency
Hyped top models can underperform on your specific task

question: How do drift and changing data affect the golden dataset over time, and what should I do about it?
reference_answer: As business data, policies and user behaviour change, a fixed golden dataset stops representing reality and offline scores mislead. The response is to monitor production continuously (online evals with baselines and drift alerts) and keep adding production failures to the golden dataset so it evolves. Drift can't be prevented, only detected and handled.
claims: Drift is always present in deployed systems and cannot be assumed away
The golden dataset represents the distribution at creation time and becomes stale
Online monitoring with baselines detects drift
Production failures are added into the golden dataset to keep it current

question: How are latency and cost treated as evals throughout the course?
reference_answer: Latency and cost belong to the operations risk category. Online they are captured signals (latency, tokens, cost) logged and dashboarded with alerts. During model selection they become requirements: cost ceiling from tokens and traffic, and a latency target based on how the product is used, both applied when shortlisting models.
claims: Latency, cost per request and token efficiency are operations risks
Online, they are captured signals sent to dashboards and alerts
In model selection, cost ceiling and latency limits become requirements
Cost is estimated from input/output tokens, price and request volume
Latency importance depends on the application

question: How are safety evaluations handled across the course?
reference_answer: Safety is one of the three risk categories, covering toxicity, harmful content, bias, PII leakage and prompt injection/jailbreak resistance. It needs application-level guardrails as well as model guardrails. In RAG, safety evals are a separate step, and online they run as computed evaluators (PII leakage, toxicity, bias, prompt injection) on sampled traffic.
claims: Safety covers toxicity, harmful content, bias, PII leakage and jailbreak/prompt-injection resistance
Guardrails are needed at application level, not just at LLM level
Safety gets its own evals in the RAG eval suite
Online safety evaluators like PII leakage or toxicity can run on sampled production traffic

question: How do reference-free evals apply to online monitoring and the RAG triad?
reference_answer: Reference-free evaluation needs no golden answer, only the inputs and outputs. Online monitoring depends on it because production has no answer key, e.g. faithfulness judged from the context and answer. The RAG triad's three metrics are also computed from question, context and answer alone, so they can be used in both offline and online settings.
claims: Reference-free evals don't use an answer key in the golden data
Online evals are reference-free because live traffic has no correct answers
Faithfulness is computed from context and answer only
The RAG triad metrics use the question, context and answer
The same metrics can run offline and online

question: What would a good structured answer to 'How do you evaluate a RAG chatbot?' include?
reference_answer: Describe an eval suite at three levels (component: retriever and generator metrics; pipeline: RAG triad; application: correctness, completeness, safety, operations), then regression testing against a baseline (basic, experiment tracking or CI gating), deployment, and online evals with tracing, drift detection and alerting, feeding failures back into the offline dataset.
claims: Explain component, pipeline and application levels with the metrics of each
Include safety and operations evals
Mention regression testing and its levels
After deployment, run online evals (tracing, computed metrics, drift, alerting)
Feed failures back into the offline dataset

question: How do I fairly compare two versions or two models of my system?
reference_answer: Run the same eval on both, with the same golden dataset and identical conditions (for models, the same run configuration). Repeat for prompts, models, re-rankers, vector databases or architectures, and compare scores; in regression testing, compare the metric report against the previous baseline.
claims: Use the same golden dataset for all versions
Keep conditions identical across candidates (same prompt/settings)
Offline evals let you compare models, prompts, re-rankers, vector databases and architectures
Regression testing compares new metrics with the previous baseline

question: What's the difference between model evals and application evals?
reference_answer: Model evals test the LLM's own capabilities (reasoning, coding, knowledge etc.) with benchmarks and are mainly done by frontier labs. Application evals test an LLM-powered product, either as a whole or by component (retriever, prompts, latency, safety), and are what AI engineers mainly do. Model evals answer 'can the model do it'; application evals answer 'does our product work'.
claims: Model evals evaluate the LLM itself and its capabilities
Application evals evaluate the LLM-based application as a whole or by component
Model evals use benchmarks and are done mostly by frontier labs
Application evals are the main day-to-day work of AI engineers
Model evals ask 'can the model do this', application evals ask 'will our product work'

question: How do offline evals differ from online evals?
reference_answer: Offline evals run before deployment on a fixed golden dataset with an answer key and anticipated inputs; they are cheap, fast and repeatable, and suit gating, version comparison and regression catching. Online evals run after deployment on live traffic with no answer key and unanticipated inputs; they can be costly at scale (so sampled), and catch drift, emergent bugs and surprises. Offline checks correctness; online checks normal operation. They complement each other.
claims: Offline runs before deployment; online runs after deployment on live traffic
Offline uses a fixed golden dataset with an answer key; online has no fixed dataset or answer key
Offline inputs are anticipated; online inputs cannot be anticipated
Offline suits gating, version comparison and regression; online suits drift detection and real-world behaviour
Offline is fast and cheap; online can be costly at scale so sampling is used
They are complementary, not rivals

question: Why do I need custom model evals when benchmarks already exist? How are they different?
reference_answer: Benchmarks are standardised public tests of generic capabilities that let you compare models on common ground. Custom evals use your own data and task, so they show how a model performs for your application, including accuracy, cost and latency. A cheaper smaller model can lose on every benchmark yet win on your task.
claims: Benchmarks are standardised shared tests for generic capabilities
Custom evals use your own dataset and application-specific scoring
Benchmarks alone can rank a costly model on top while a cheaper model is better value for your task
Custom evals reveal task-specific accuracy, cost and latency

question: What's the difference between reference-based and reference-free evaluation?
reference_answer: Reference-based evaluation compares outputs with a known correct answer or key content stored in the golden dataset (e.g. retriever recall, UPSC marks by human graders). Reference-free evaluation has no correct answer; it judges using a rubric or the inputs and outputs alone (e.g. helpfulness rubric, faithfulness, online hallucination checks). Test: does your golden dataset contain the correct answer?
claims: Reference-based: the correct answer or key points are written down for each test case
Reference-free: no correct answer is stored; a rubric or input/output-based judgement is used
Retriever recall and human-graded marks are reference-based
Helpfulness rubrics and online hallucination or faithfulness checks are reference-free
Simple test: is the correct answer present in the golden dataset?

question: When should I use a programmatic eval, a human eval or an LLM judge?
reference_answer: Programmatic evals are cheap, fast and deterministic, suited for measurable things like accuracy or recall; they can't judge nuanced qualities like helpfulness or long text. Human evals are the most reliable but costly, so they don't scale. LLM-as-a-judge is the middle ground for nuanced judgements at scale, though it needs a rubric and validation against humans.
claims: Programmatic: cheap and automatic, but limited to things computable by code
Human: reliable and trusted, but expensive and hard to scale
LLM judge: handles nuanced text judgements at a fraction of the cost of humans
LLM judges need clear rubrics and validation against human judgement

question: What's the difference between precision and recall for a RAG retriever?
reference_answer: Recall asks how many of the relevant documents that exist were retrieved in the top K. Precision asks how many of the retrieved documents were actually useful. A retriever can have high recall but low precision (retrieves everything relevant plus junk) or the reverse, so both are measured.
claims: Recall = how many of the right documents were retrieved
Precision = how many of the retrieved documents were useful
Both measure different aspects of retriever relevance
Both are evaluated at component level in the RAG eval suite

question: How do context relevance, faithfulness and answer relevance differ?
reference_answer: Context relevance links question and retrieved context: is the fetched context relevant to the question? Faithfulness links answer and context: is the answer grounded in that context or hallucinated? Answer relevance links answer and question: does the answer address what was asked?
claims: Context relevance: question vs retrieved context
Faithfulness: answer vs context, checking for hallucination
Answer relevance: answer vs question
Together they form the RAG triad

question: What are captured signals versus computed signals in online evals?
reference_answer: Captured signals are recorded as they occur, needing no calculation (thumbs up/down, latency, cost, token usage), so they flow from logs to a dashboard and alerts. Computed signals must be derived by an evaluator (faithfulness, answer relevance, correctness, hallucination, toxicity, bias), so they need sampling and an evaluator such as an LLM judge before dashboarding.
claims: Captured signals are stored directly, e.g. thumbs, latency, cost, tokens
Captured signals go straight to dashboards and alerts
Computed signals must be calculated by an evaluator, e.g. faithfulness, hallucination, toxicity, bias
Computed signals need sampling and an evaluator step

question: How do component-level, workflow-level and application-level failures differ?
reference_answer: Component failures happen in one part (retriever, generator, reranker, parser). Workflow failures arise from how components interact even if each works alone. Application failures concern the whole system, such as latency, cost or time to first token. Each level needs its own evals.
claims: Component-level failures are in individual parts
Workflow-level failures arise from interactions even when components pass individually
Application-level failures concern whole-system properties like latency and cost
Each level requires its own eval

question: How is testing an LLM application different from ordinary software testing?
reference_answer: Software is deterministic: the same input always gives the same output, and you mostly check correctness. LLM apps are probabilistic: the same input can give different valid outputs, and there's no single definition of correctness, so you check multiple aspects such as grounding, safety, latency, cost, style and answer quality, using rubrics.

The same LLM input can produce different outputs that are all acceptable
Software correctness is simple, whereas LLM correctness has many dimensions
LLM evaluation needs multiple criteria like safety, latency, cost, groundedness and style
This makes LLM evaluation much trickier than software testing

question: What's the difference between benchmark contamination and benchmark saturation?
reference_answer: Contamination is when benchmark questions and answers leak into a model's training data so scores are inflated by memorisation. Saturation is when models score so well (often partly because of contamination and improvement) that top models cluster and the benchmark can no longer distinguish them.
claims: Contamination: benchmark data leaks into training data and inflates scores
Saturation: top models cluster at similar high scores so the benchmark is no longer discriminative
Contamination can contribute to saturation
Saturated benchmarks are retired

question: How does MMLU-Pro differ from MMLU?
reference_answer: MMLU-Pro is an upgrade that fixes MMLU's flaws: 10 answer options instead of 4, basic and noisy questions replaced with reasoning-based ones, and fewer, better balanced categories (14 disciplines, about 12,000 questions). It favours reasoning models and is nearing saturation, and it has no human baseline.
claims: MMLU-Pro uses 10 options instead of 4
It removes basic factual and noisy questions and adds reasoning questions
It uses fewer, balanced disciplines than MMLU's 57 subjects
Reasoning models score noticeably higher on it
It has no human baseline and is approaching saturation

question: How does SimpleQA compare with TruthfulQA?
reference_answer: Both target reliability. TruthfulQA (2021) is a multiple-choice test of common misconceptions and became saturated. SimpleQA (2024) asks short factual questions with no options, graded by an LLM as correct, incorrect or not attempted, so it tests factuality and calibration. It replaced TruthfulQA and remains active.
claims: TruthfulQA targets misconceptions with selected answers; SimpleQA asks open short factual questions
SimpleQA grades correct, incorrect or not attempted, capturing calibration
TruthfulQA saturated while SimpleQA is still active
SimpleQA replaced TruthfulQA as the reliability benchmark

question: What are pass@1, pass@k and majority@k?
reference_answer: Pass@1 asks the model once per question and counts it right or wrong (strict). Pass@k asks k times and counts success if at least one attempt is right (lenient). Majority@k asks k times and takes the most frequent answer (the mode). Benchmarks must state which is used, and it must be constant across compared models.
claims: Pass@1: single attempt, strict
Pass@k: correct if any of k attempts is correct, more lenient
Majority@k: the most common answer among k attempts is taken
The strategy must be stated and kept the same when comparing models

question: Are leaderboards a selection tool or a filtering tool, and how does that compare to custom evals?
reference_answer: Leaderboards are a filtering tool, not a decision tool: they narrow down 100+ models to 3-5 or 5-10 candidates that fit your requirements. The decision comes from running your own custom evals on those candidates with your data and task.
claims: Leaderboards filter candidates instead of deciding the final model
They shortlist a handful of models from many
Custom evals on your own data make the final decision
Leaderboard ranking alone should not be the reason for choosing a model
